Both Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are types of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that cause chronic inflammation of the digestive tract.
Ulcerative colitis**: Inflammation is limited to the colon (large intestine) and affects only the inner surface (mucosal layer) of that organ.

Crohn’s disease**: Inflammation can occur anywhere along the digestive tract—from the mouth to the anus—but most commonly involves the small intestine (especially the ileum) and the beginning of the large intestine.
Ulcerative colitis**: Involves only the inner lining (mucosa) of the colon.
Crohn’s disease**: Extends deeper into the intestinal wall, affecting multiple layers of tissue.

The two disorders show different patterns: ulcerative colitis produces a continuous area of inflammation limited to the colon, whereas Crohn’s disease often has “skip lesions” (patchy areas of inflammation) and can affect any part of the GI tract.
Crohn’s disease** may lead to intestinal blockage, fistulas, and extra‑intestinal problems such as joint, eye, or skin issues.
Ulcerative colitis** primarily causes bleeding, pus, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort due to loss of the colon lining.
